pack.name: correlation
pack.description: Cross-platform rules that correlate independent findings and inventory.

false_positives: Legacy device management on an isolated network.
A different service that happens to use one of these ports.
confidence_boosters: The listening process name matching the protocol.
Firewall rules allowing the port from untrusted networks.
rules.name: Cleartext remote-access service listening on a non-loopback address
rules.description: A telnet, FTP, TFTP or r-service port is listening on an address other than loopback.
rules.severity_reason: These protocols send credentials or data unprotected, and TFTP has no authentication at all.
rules.confidence_reason: The port number identifies the usual service; the process may be something else, and reachability depends on filtering.

clauses.description: A cleartext-protocol port bound to a non-loopback address

rules.title: Cleartext service port {lst.attrs.port} listening on {lst.attrs.bind}
rules.rationale: Cleartext remote-access protocols expose credentials to anyone on the path and are frequent entry points; a listener on a routable address makes them reachable.
investigation: Identify the owning process and package.
Check firewall policy for the port.
Review authentication logs for the service.
rules.remediation: Replace with SSH/SFTP (or restrict to a management network) and disable the service once confirmed unnecessary.

attack.explanation: An exposed remote-access service can serve as an external access point; exposure to attackers is not established.

examples.name: windows ftp service on IPv6 wildcard

confidence_boosters: Change tickets for the account added.
Logon activity of the added account.
rules.name: Membership of a privileged group changed
rules.description: Since the previous snapshot the membership of an administrative group (sudo, wheel, admin, root, local Administrators) changed.
rules.severity_reason: Administrative group membership grants full control; any change should be explainable by an approved request.
rules.confidence_reason: The change is exact; most such changes are legitimate administration.

clauses.description: A privileged group record whose members changed

rules.title: Privileged group membership changed: {grp.key}
rules.rationale: Adding an account to sudo/wheel/Administrators is the simplest privilege escalation once someone can edit group files, and it is easy to overlook between assessments.
investigation: Compare the before and after member lists in the detail of the contributing change.
Check the account's creation time and recent logons.
Confirm the change against an approved request.
rules.remediation: Remove unauthorised members, reset their credentials and review what they accessed; document approved changes.

attack.explanation: Changing group membership is a form of account manipulation to maintain or elevate access; it is also routine administration.

false_positives: Competition or lab hosts configured deliberately weak.
confidence_boosters: Evidence that the weak control applies to the privileged account (for example sshd allowing that account).
Logons by the privileged account from unusual sources.
rules.name: Privileged-account anomaly together with weak authentication settings
rules.description: An unexpected or over-privileged account configuration was found on a host that also has weak authentication controls.
rules.severity_reason: Each side is a configuration concern; together they widen the path from a guessed or missing credential to administrative access. Severity is raised only when the weak control can be bypassed outright.

severity_rules.reason: An authentication-bypass-class weakness (PAM accepts without credential, passwordless accounts, no NLA, auto-logon) is present.

rules.confidence_reason: Both sides are exact findings; their relationship (same accounts, reachable service) is not established by the data.
rules.title: Privileged-account anomaly with weak authentication on {host}
rules.rationale: An attacker needs a way to authenticate and a privileged identity to use. Seeing a questionable privileged account and weak authentication on one host is more actionable than either alone.
investigation: Check whether the privileged account can use the weak authentication path (sshd AllowUsers, PAM stack for the service).
Review authentication logs for the privileged accounts.
Fix the bypass-class weakness first.
rules.remediation: Remove or justify the anomalous privileged account, then close the authentication weakness (PAM/sshd/NLA/lockout) in the order of the severity rationale.

attack.explanation: Valid accounts are often used with weak authentication to gain access; nothing here shows use.
Account manipulation is one way a privileged anomaly arises.

examples.name: anomaly with lockout missing is medium
windows hidden admin plus no NLA

false_positives: Hosts protected by a dedicated upstream firewall and reachable only from a management VLAN.
confidence_boosters: Confirmation from network scans or upstream ACLs that the ports are reachable.
Firewall configuration changes since the previous snapshot.
rules.name: Host firewall absent or permissive while management or data services listen
rules.description: The host firewall is disabled, default-allow, or allows everything inbound, and remote-management or database ports are listening on non-loopback addresses.
rules.severity_reason: With no effective host filtering, every listed service is reachable by anything that can route to the host.
rules.confidence_reason: Both facts are exact; a network firewall in front of the host may still provide protection that is not visible here.

clauses.description: Host firewall disabled, default-allow or allow-all
A management or data port listening on a non-loopback address

rules.title: Open host firewall with listening management/data services
rules.rationale: A host firewall is the last filter for services bound to every interface. Its absence plus a listening management or database port is a concrete exposure, not just a hygiene gap.
investigation: Verify reachability of the listed ports from an untrusted segment.
Check upstream filtering and the firewall change history.
Identify owners of the listening services.
rules.remediation: Enable the host firewall with an allow-list for required ports (reload rather than flush; verify scored ports first), or bind the services to loopback.

attack.explanation: Exposed services without filtering enlarge the attack surface for exploitation of public-facing applications; none is exploited here.

examples.name: windows firewall off with RDP and SMB listening
firewall open but only ssh listens
redis on loopback with open firewall

false_positives: Software legitimately installed under ProgramData or /opt that is also unsigned or recently updated.
confidence_boosters: Hash and signature of the file; creation time relative to the startup entry.
Network connections made by the process started from this path.
rules.name: Persistence entry executes a file that the filesystem checks also flagged
rules.description: A service, task, autorun, cron job or unit refers to a path that a filesystem finding (world-writable, temporary, unsigned, hidden or recently modified executable) also lists.
rules.severity_reason: A startup mechanism that points at a file sitting in an unsafe place or flagged as unusual is the shape of a planted foothold.
rules.confidence_reason: Linking is by a shared path string in two independent findings; the path is exact but the file's purpose is still unknown.

clauses.description: A suspicious service, task, autorun or cron/unit finding
A filesystem finding about an unusual executable or writable file

rules.title: Persistence entry runs a file flagged by the filesystem checks: {file.evidence.paths}
rules.rationale: Two independent collectors (startup configuration and file inspection) describe the same path. That agreement is stronger than either finding alone and shows where to look first.
investigation: Open the shared path: owner, hash, signature, timestamps.
Read the startup entry that references it.
Check whether other entries reference the same path.
rules.remediation: Preserve the file and the entry as evidence, disable the startup entry, then remove or restore the file from a trusted source.

attack.explanation: Service/unit persistence can launch attacker-placed files; here the link is only a shared path.
Scheduled execution can launch attacker-placed files; here the link is only a shared path.

examples.name: unit executes file in /tmp that is also flagged
persistence finding without a filesystem finding
case differences in paths still join

false_positives: Planned deployment of a new service with its firewall rule.
confidence_boosters: Change tickets for the new service.
The process name and package of the new listener.
rules.name: Firewall configuration changed and a new non-loopback listener appeared
rules.description: Between two snapshots the host firewall configuration changed and a new listener on a non-loopback address appeared.
rules.severity_reason: Either change can be routine administration; the combination warrants review, not alarm.
rules.confidence_reason: Both changes are exact; the ordering and the relationship between them are not known from two point-in-time snapshots.
rules.title: Firewall changed and new listener appeared: {lst.key}
rules.rationale: Opening a firewall path and starting a listener are two halves of exposing a service. Seeing both since the last snapshot is worth confirming against change records.
investigation: Compare the firewall record's before/after attributes.
Identify the process and package behind the new listener.
Confirm both against change records.
rules.remediation: Revert the firewall change and stop the service if unplanned; otherwise record the change and update the baseline.

attack.explanation: Modifying the host firewall is a defence-evasion technique; the change here may be legitimate.

false_positives: Provisioning or configuration-management runs that create a service account and its job.
confidence_boosters: The account owning or referenced by the job.
A recorded change request covering both.
rules.name: Scheduled-job change together with an account or group change
rules.description: Since the previous snapshot a scheduled job (cron entry or non-Microsoft task) was added or modified and a user or group record was also added or modified.
rules.severity_reason: New scheduled execution plus a new or changed account is a common attacker sequence, but also routine onboarding; severity is not raised further.
rules.confidence_reason: Two point-in-time changes with no proof they are related; the rule excludes built-in Microsoft task churn to reduce noise.

clauses.description: A scheduled job added or modified (not a built-in Windows task)
A user added or modified, or group membership changed

rules.title: Scheduled job and account changes appeared together ({job.key}, {acct.key})
rules.rationale: Persistence and access are often established together: a new account to log in with and a scheduled job to keep code running. Neither alone is notable; together they merit a look.
investigation: Read the job's command and schedule; check the account named in it.
Compare the account's attributes before and after.
Check authentication logs for the new or changed account.
rules.remediation: If unplanned, disable the job and the account after preserving evidence; otherwise update the baseline.

attack.explanation: Scheduled execution is a persistence technique; the job here may be benign.
Account creation is a persistence technique; the account here may be benign.

false_positives: Hosts using centralised authentication (LDAP/SSSD/AD) where local policy is intentionally minimal.
confidence_boosters: Confirmation that no central policy compensates.
rules.name: Multiple authentication-configuration weaknesses
rules.description: Three or more different authentication-related weaknesses (PAM, sshd, password policy, lockout, RDP) are present on one host.
rules.severity_reason: Each weakness is individually low or medium; together they leave credential guessing unthrottled and unchecked. Severity is deliberately not raised for the count.
rules.confidence_reason: The findings are accurate individually; the rule only counts distinct weaknesses.
rules.title: Several authentication weaknesses on {host}
rules.rationale: Password guessing and credential reuse succeed where policy, lockout and hashing are all weak. The grouping shows a systemic gap rather than one oversight.
investigation: List the distinct findings and decide which gap to close first (bypass-class first).
Check authentication logs for guessing patterns.
Confirm whether central authentication policy applies.
rules.remediation: Enforce a password-quality module, account lockout, strong hashing and secure sshd/RDP settings; coordinate with scored-service account owners first.

attack.explanation: Weak lockout and password policy facilitate brute-force attacks; none is observed.

false_positives: Hosts with custom logging pipelines that look impaired to the collector, plus an unrelated admin script flagged as persistence.
confidence_boosters: Timestamps showing the persistence artefact was created after logging was reduced.
rules.name: Logging or protection impaired alongside a persistence indicator
rules.description: A log-impairment or protection-disabling finding appears on the same host as a high-signal persistence finding.
rules.severity_reason: Persistence indicators are concerning on their own; paired with reduced logging or protection they suggest the host was prepared to avoid detection.
rules.confidence_reason: Both are accurate findings; their link is that they co-occur, not that one caused the other.
rules.title: Reduced logging/protection together with a persistence indicator
rules.rationale: Attackers who establish persistence commonly also reduce what is recorded. Co-occurrence prioritises this host for investigation over hosts with only one of the signals.
investigation: Establish the timeline from file and configuration timestamps.
Check whether other hosts show the same pair.
Collect volatile evidence (processes, connections) before changing anything.
rules.remediation: Restore logging and protection, preserve and then remove the persistence artefact, and review the host for further changes.

attack.explanation: Impairing defences is a tactic used alongside persistence; co-occurrence here does not prove it.

examples.name: windows event log service off plus WMI consumer
